questions.q: In the Figure/Axes model, what is the key difference between `fig` and `ax` after running `fig, ax = plt.subplots()`?
options: `fig` is the overall canvas/container you save or show, while `ax` is the specific plotting surface you call drawing methods like `.plot()` and `.set_xlabel()` on
`fig` and `ax` are two interchangeable names for the exact same object
`ax` is only used for 3D plots, while `fig` is used for all 2D plots
`fig` controls colors and `ax` controls text, with no other distinction between them
questions.explain: `fig` is the whole canvas (what you call `savefig` on), and `ax` is an individual plotting area where `.plot()`, `.bar()`, `.set_title()`, and similar methods are called.

questions.q: You call `ax.plot(x, y)` with no `label=` argument, then call `ax.legend()`. What happens?
options: The legend either doesn't appear or appears empty, because `ax.legend()` builds its entries from each plotted series' `label=` argument, which was never set
Matplotlib automatically labels the series using the variable name `y`
An error is raised immediately because `label=` is a required argument to `.plot()`
The legend appears but shows a random color swatch with no text at all times
questions.explain: The legend is built from each plot call's `label=` keyword; a series plotted without a `label` simply doesn't contribute an entry to the legend.

questions.q: With `axes = plt.subplots(1, 3)[1]` (a 1-row, 3-column grid), how do you reference the middle panel's Axes object?
options: `axes[1]`, since with a single row, `axes` is returned as a 1D array indexed by column position
`axes[0, 1]`, since `axes` is always a 2D array regardless of grid shape
`axes.middle`, a named attribute Matplotlib creates automatically
`axes[2]`, because subplot grids are always indexed starting from the last panel
questions.explain: For a grid with exactly one row (or one column), `plt.subplots` returns a 1D array of Axes, so the middle of three panels is `axes[1]`; a 2D indexing scheme like `axes[row, col]` only applies once the grid has more than one row and more than one column.

questions.q: What does `fig.savefig("plot.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")` specifically control, beyond just writing the file?
options: `dpi` sets the image resolution (sharper lines/text at higher values) and `bbox_inches="tight"` trims excess whitespace so labels aren't cut off at the edges
`dpi` sets the file format and `bbox_inches` sets the plot's title text
Both arguments are purely cosmetic legacy options with no visible effect in current Matplotlib versions
`dpi` controls the legend's font size and `bbox_inches` controls the color palette
questions.explain: `dpi` (dots per inch) governs image sharpness/resolution, and `bbox_inches="tight"` recalculates the saved image's bounding box so axis labels and titles near the edges aren't clipped.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend the object-oriented style (`fig, ax = plt.subplots()` then `ax.plot(...)`) over the older `plt.plot(...)` shortcut style?
options: The object-oriented style scales cleanly to figures with multiple panels, since each Axes object is addressed individually, whereas the shortcut style gets ambiguous once there's more than one panel
The `plt.plot(...)` shortcut style has been completely removed from current Matplotlib versions
The object-oriented style is required for line plots but cannot be used for bar charts
There is no real difference; the recommendation is purely a matter of personal preference with no practical consequence
questions.explain: The shortcut `plt.plot(...)` style implicitly acts on 'the current axes,' which becomes confusing once a figure has multiple panels; explicitly calling methods on a named `ax` (or `axes[i]`) object avoids that ambiguity.
